title: Choosing a Rendering Strategy per Page
objectives: Match static, server, client and streamed rendering to how fresh and personal a page is
Use revalidation, streaming and partial hydration to mix strategies on one site
Explain the cost each strategy moves to the build, the server or the device

cards.title: Ask two questions per page
cards.body: How often does the content change, and does it differ per user? A blog post changes rarely and is the same for everyone, so build it once as static HTML. A logged-in dashboard is personal and changes every minute, so render it per request or on the client. Most sites need several answers, one per kind of page.

cards.title: Worked example: a shop with 50,000 products
cards.body: Product pages are public and change a few times a day, which suits static HTML. Rebuilding 50,000 pages at 20 ms each takes 1,000 s, about 17 minutes, too slow for every price change. Instead, regenerate just the affected page when its price changes, and keep a maximum age of a few minutes as a backstop in case a change event is missed. The cart is personal, so it renders on the client.

cards.title: Picking per page
cards.body: Freshness and personalisation decide; the rest is tuning.
steps: Same for everyone and changes rarely: build static HTML
Same for everyone but changes often: static with background revalidation
Personal but must show content fast: render on the server per request, streaming slow parts
Highly interactive after login: render on the client
Mostly static with a few interactive widgets: hydrate only those widgets

cards.title: Streaming and partial hydration
cards.body: Streaming sends the page shell and fast sections first, then fills slow sections as their data arrives, so one slow query does not hold back the whole page. Partial hydration, sometimes called islands, ships script only for the interactive parts of a mostly static page, so the device runs less code before it can respond.

cards.title: Trap: one strategy for the whole site
cards.body: Rendering every page on the client makes public pages slow to show and harder for crawlers; rendering every page per request on the server pays server time for pages that never change. Choose per route, and measure the pages that matter most.

questions.prompt: A documentation site has 2,000 pages, the same for every reader, updated weekly. Which strategy fits best?

choices.label: Render each page per request on the server
Render everything on the client after login
Build static HTML and serve it from a CDN
Stream each page section by section

questions.explanation: Unchanging, shared content is cheapest and fastest as prebuilt files.

questions.prompt: Prices on 50,000 product pages change a few times a day. What keeps pages fast and reasonably fresh?

choices.label: Static pages regenerated when their price changes
A full rebuild of every page whenever any price changes
Client rendering with no HTML from the server
Server rendering with caching turned off

questions.explanation: Regenerating a page when its data changes keeps it cached and correct; an age limit is the backstop.

questions.prompt: An account page has a fast header and a slow order-history query. How can the header show sooner?

choices.label: Cache the slow query in the browser forever
Stream the shell first and fill the order history when ready
Wait for both queries, then send the complete page in one go
Move the whole page to static HTML

questions.explanation: Streaming decouples fast and slow sections of one response.

questions.prompt: A marketing page is static except for a newsletter form and an image carousel. What reduces the script the device runs?

choices.label: Hydrating the whole page as one application
Rendering the page on the client instead
Inlining all scripts into the HTML
Hydrating only the form and the carousel

questions.explanation: Partial hydration ships code only for the parts that need it.

questions.prompt: Order these pages from most static to most dynamic rendering.

items.label: A personalised home feed
An “About us” page
A live trading dashboard
A product page with prices

questions.explanation: Rarely changing shared pages build statically; personal, live pages render per request or on the client.

questions.prompt: A full static build takes 20 ms per page. About how many minutes does rebuilding 50,000 pages take?
assumptions: Pages build one at a time
questions.formula: 50,000 pages at 20 ms each, in minutes
questions.explanation: Sanity check: too slow to rebuild on each price change, which is why per-page revalidation exists.

flashcards.back: How often it changes, and whether it differs per user.
Serve cached static HTML; regenerate it after it is older than a set age.
Hydrate only the interactive parts of a mostly static page.

mechanism.title: Where each strategy does its work
steps: Static generation renders HTML at build time. Requests are served from files, often on a CDN, so time to first byte is low and servers do little. The cost is the build: content is only as fresh as the last build, and very large sites take long to rebuild.

Revalidation narrows that gap. A page is served from cache until it is older than a set age; the next request still gets the cached copy while the page regenerates in the background. HTTP has a matching idea in the stale-while-revalidate cache directive. Some platforms also allow regenerating a page on demand when its data changes. Age alone gives no freshness bound for rarely visited pages: the first visitor after hours still gets the old copy, so pages whose data must be correct are also regenerated on demand when that data changes.

Server rendering per request builds HTML with fresh, personal data. The server pays for every request, and time to first byte includes the slowest data fetch unless the response is streamed. Streaming sends the shell and ready sections first and appends the rest in the same response as data arrives.

Client rendering sends a small HTML shell and script that fetches data and builds the page in the browser. After the first load, navigation can be quick, but the first view waits for script to download and run, and slower devices feel it most.

Hydration attaches behaviour to server-rendered HTML, which means running the page’s components on the device. Partial or progressive hydration limits that work to the interactive parts, or delays it until they are visible or used, reducing script cost on content-heavy pages.

useWhen: Sites with different kinds of page: public catalogue, personal account, interactive tools.
Pages where both first view speed and interactivity matter.
avoidWhen: Avoid client-only rendering for public pages that must show fast and be crawled.
Avoid per-request server rendering for content that is the same for everyone and rarely changes.

rows: A change event per update, plus an age backstop
Script download and run on the device

numbers.title: Rebuild everything or revalidate per page?
assumptions: Prices change a few times a day
steps: Full rebuild: 50,000 pages at 20 ms each is 1,000 s, about 17 minutes.
A price change would wait up to 17 minutes plus deploy time.
Regenerating a page when its price changes renders only changed pages, within seconds of the change.
Age-based revalidation alone would let a page nobody visited for 3 hours show a 3-hour-old price to the next shopper.
numbers.result: Regenerate on change with a short age as a backstop: large catalogues stay correct without full rebuilds or per-request rendering.

india.title: How the guidance frames it
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The web.dev article on rendering on the web compares static rendering, server rendering, client rendering and hydration, and notes that server and static rendering can show content sooner while full client rendering and heavy hydration add script cost on the device. MDN documents the stale-while-revalidate directive of Cache-Control, which lets a cache serve a stale response while it fetches a fresh one in the background.

pitfalls.trap: “Server rendering is faster, so render everything per request.”
pitfalls.say: “Static is faster still for shared content; I’d choose per page by freshness and personalisation.”

pitfalls.trap: “Hydration is free once the HTML is there.”
pitfalls.say: “Hydration runs component code on the device; I’d limit it to the interactive parts.”

takeaways: Choose rendering per page by freshness and personalisation.
Revalidation keeps static pages fresh without full rebuilds.
Streaming stops one slow section from delaying the whole page.
Hydrate only what must be interactive.

interactive.title: Render the product page
interactive.prompt: A shop has 50,000 product pages viewed by anonymous shoppers. Prices change a few times a day and must be correct within about 10 minutes. How should product pages render?

choices.label: Static pages regenerated when a price changes, with a 5-minute age as a backstop
choices.feedback: Right: shared content is served from cache, each page is rebuilt when its price changes, and the age catches a missed update.

choices.label: Render each page on the server for every request, without a cache
choices.feedback: Fresh, but every view pays server time for content that is the same for everyone.

choices.label: Render on the client from a product API once the script has loaded
choices.feedback: Shoppers and crawlers wait for script before seeing the product; slower phones suffer most.

interactive.reveal: Age-based revalidation alone is not enough here: a rarely viewed page keeps its old price until someone visits after it goes stale, and that visitor still sees the old copy. Regenerating on change gives the 10-minute bound. The cart and account sections are personal, so they render on the client or per request. One site, several strategies.

seeAlso.why: The critical rendering path each strategy feeds

title: Optimistic UI and Rolling Back Conflicts
objectives: Show the result of an action before the server confirms it, and know when not to
Roll back cleanly on errors and on 409 or 412 conflicts
Use versions so concurrent edits are detected instead of overwritten

cards.title: Assume success, prepare to undo
cards.body: An optimistic update changes the screen as soon as the user acts, then sends the request. If the server agrees, nothing more happens. If it fails, the interface restores the previous state and says what went wrong. For likes, renames and reordering this makes the app feel instant.

cards.title: Worked example: two people rename one card
cards.body: Asha and Ben both open card 42 at version 7. Asha renames it; her request says “if version is 7” and succeeds, making version 8. Ben’s rename also says “if version is 7”, so the server answers 412 Precondition Failed. Ben’s screen had already shown his title, so it rolls back, refetches the card, shows Asha’s title and offers to apply his change again.

cards.title: Life of an optimistic edit
cards.body: Keep what you need to undo until the server answers.
steps: Save a snapshot of the item and its version
Apply the change on screen at once
Send the request with the version it was based on
On success, store the server’s new version
On failure or conflict, restore the confirmed state (refetch on conflict) and explain

cards.title: When not to be optimistic
cards.body: Payments, bookings and anything the user cannot easily undo should wait for the server. So should actions that often fail validation on the server. Showing a success that later disappears is worse than a short spinner when the stakes are high.

cards.title: Trap: rolling back to a stale snapshot
cards.body: If two optimistic edits to one item are in flight and the first fails, restoring the snapshot taken before it can wipe the second edit too. Track pending changes per item, or refetch the item from the server after a failure instead of guessing.

questions.prompt: Which action is the best fit for an optimistic update?

choices.label: Paying for an order
Starring a message
Transferring money between accounts
Booking the last seat on a flight

questions.explanation: Low stakes, rarely fails, and easy to undo on screen.

questions.prompt: A save sends “If-Match” with the version it read, and another user saved first. What should the server reply?

choices.label: 200 OK, saving it over the other user’s earlier change
404 Not Found
412 Precondition Failed, so the client can resolve
500 Internal Server Error

questions.explanation: The precondition was a version that no longer matches; the client must reconcile.

questions.prompt: An optimistic rename fails with a network error. What should the interface do?

choices.label: Restore the previous name and let the user retry
Keep the new name and hope the next save works
Reload the whole page without a message
Show the new name greyed out with no explanation

questions.explanation: Roll back to the confirmed state and make the failure visible.

questions.prompt: Why send the version you read with each update?

choices.label: It makes the request smaller
It lets the server and CDN cache the response for longer
It replaces the need for authentication
It lets the server detect an edit based on old data

questions.explanation: Without it, the last request silently overwrites the earlier one.

questions.prompt: Order an optimistic update that may conflict.

items.label: Send it with the version it was based on
Snapshot the item and its version
Roll back and explain on 409 or 412
Show the change at once, before sending

questions.explanation: Snapshot first so there is something to restore, show the change, then send it with its version.

questions.prompt: A like request takes 300 ms. A user likes 20 posts while scrolling. About how many seconds of spinners does an optimistic design save them in total?
questions.workedAnswer: 6,000 ms is 6 s of waiting removed
questions.explanation: Sanity check: small per action, but it is the feeling of lag on every tap that optimistic updates remove.

flashcards.back: Show the result at once, send the request, undo on failure.
Someone changed it first; roll back, show their version, offer to reapply.
Payments, bookings and other costly or often-rejected actions.

mechanism.title: How an optimistic update stays correct
steps: The client keeps two views of an item: the last state the server confirmed and the state with pending local changes applied. The screen shows the second. Each pending change records what it changed so it can be undone or reapplied.

The request carries the version the change was based on. Over HTTP this is often an entity tag sent in If-Match, or a version number in the body. The server applies the change only if the stored version still matches, then returns the new version.

If another write happened first, the server rejects the request: 412 Precondition Failed when an If-Match precondition fails, or 409 Conflict when the application detects the clash itself. The client then drops its pending change, takes the server’s current state and decides: reapply automatically if the changes touch different fields, or ask the user.

Network errors and timeouts are less clear: the write may or may not have happened. Sending an idempotency key with the request lets the client retry safely, and refetching the item settles what the server holds before the screen is corrected.

Several pending edits to one item should be applied in order on top of the confirmed state. When one fails, rebuild the shown state from the confirmed state plus the remaining pending edits, rather than restoring a snapshot that predates them. Whatever happens, the user should see a short message that names the change that was undone and why, so a rollback never looks like a glitch or lost work.

useWhen: Frequent, low-stakes actions such as likes, renames, reordering and toggles.
Collaborative apps where edits are usually accepted.
avoidWhen: Avoid for payments, bookings and irreversible actions.
Avoid when the server often rejects the action, so rollbacks become common.

rows: A short delay on every action

numbers.title: Waiting the user does not see
steps: Pessimistic: 20 likes at 300 ms each is 6,000 ms of spinners.
Optimistic: the screen changes at once; requests finish in the background.
If 1 in 200 likes fails, about one rollback per 10 sessions of this size.
Each rollback must be visible and explained.
numbers.result: The saving is per-tap responsiveness; the cost is a rare, explained rollback.

india.title: What the HTTP standard defines
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 9110 defines conditional requests: a client can send If-Match with an entity tag so that the server performs the method only if the resource still has that tag, and responds 412 Precondition Failed otherwise. This lets clients avoid the lost-update problem when several clients edit one resource. MDN also documents 409 Conflict for requests that conflict with the current state of the target.

pitfalls.say: “It means we show the change first and roll back visibly when the server disagrees.”
“I’d send the version so the server returns 412 instead of silently overwriting someone else.”

takeaways: Show low-stakes changes at once and undo on failure.
Send the version you read; expect 409 or 412 on conflicts.
Rebuild from confirmed state plus pending edits after a failure.
Wait for the server on costly or irreversible actions.

interactive.title: Two renames, one card
interactive.prompt: Asha and Ben both load card 42 at version 7. Asha renames it to “Launch plan” and her save succeeds. Ben, still on version 7, renames it to “Q3 launch” and his screen updates at once. What should Ben see a moment later?

choices.label: “Q3 launch”, because his save came last
choices.feedback: Only if the server ignores versions, which would silently overwrite Asha’s change.

choices.label: “Launch plan”, with a note that the card changed and an offer to reapply
choices.feedback: Right: the server rejects the stale version, and his screen rolls back to the confirmed state.

choices.label: An error page until he reloads
choices.feedback: A conflict is expected in collaborative apps; it should be handled in place.

interactive.reveal: Ben’s request carried version 7, but the card is at version 8, so the server answers 412. His client restores the server’s title and lets him decide whether his rename should replace it.

seeAlso.why: Idempotency keys for retried client requests
Server-side validation that can reject a change

title: Keeping Many Tabs in Sync
objectives: Explain why several tabs of one app drift apart
Send changes between tabs with broadcast messages and storage events
Elect one leader tab for work that should run once

cards.title: Every tab is its own app
cards.body: Each tab runs its own copy of the page with its own memory. Log out in one and the others still show the account; read a message in one and the unread badge in the others stays. Storage such as IndexedDB is shared by tabs of the same origin, but the screens only change when each tab learns that something changed.

cards.title: Worked example: logout everywhere
cards.body: A user has five tabs open and logs out in one. That tab clears its session and posts a “logged-out” message on a broadcast channel named for the app. The other four tabs receive it, clear their in-memory data and show the sign-in screen. Without the message, they would keep showing private data until their next request failed.

cards.title: Coordinating tabs
cards.body: Share data through storage, signal through messages, run shared work once.
steps: Write the change to shared storage
Post a small message to the other tabs
Other tabs reload the changed data from storage
One tab holds a lock and runs shared work, such as a live connection
When it closes, another tab acquires the lock and takes over

cards.title: One connection, not five
cards.body: If every tab opens its own live connection and polls the same API, five tabs mean five times the load. Using the Web Locks API, the tabs ask for one named lock; the tab that holds it keeps the connection and posts updates to the others. When that tab closes, the lock is released and a waiting tab takes over.

cards.title: Trap: sending whole state in every message
cards.body: Messages between tabs should say what changed, not carry the full app state. Large messages are copied into every tab, and tabs can apply them in different orders. Store the data once, send an identifier and a version, and let each tab read the current value.

questions.prompt: A user marks a chat as read in one tab. Why does another tab still show it unread?

choices.label: Each tab keeps its own in-memory state until told to refresh
The browser blocks storage for the second tab
The server pushes the read status to only the most recent tab
Browsers cache the badge for an hour

questions.explanation: Tabs share storage but not memory; something must tell the other tab to update.

questions.prompt: A brokerage dashboard is open in three tabs. An order fills in one tab. What is the lightest way to update the holdings shown in the other two?

choices.label: Every tab polls the holdings API once a second
Route a message through the server to each tab
Post a small message on a broadcast channel
Each tab re-reads a cookie once a second

questions.explanation: A broadcast channel delivers the message to every same-origin tab with no network trip; each tab then reads the new holdings from storage or refetches once. Polling from three tabs triples the load for a rare change, routing through the server adds a round trip and a connection per tab, and polling a cookie is a slow workaround from before broadcast channels.

questions.prompt: Six tabs each open a live connection to the same feed. What reduces this to one connection?

choices.label: Closing the connection when a tab is hidden
Having the server reject extra connections from the same user’s browser
Opening the connection only on page reload
One tab holds a named lock, keeps the connection and relays updates

questions.explanation: Leader election with a lock gives one connection and automatic hand-over.

questions.prompt: What should a cross-tab message about an edited note contain?

choices.label: The full application state, serialised
The note’s id and new version
The user’s session token
A full copy of every note

questions.explanation: Send what changed, the id and new version, and let each tab read the current value from shared storage, so out-of-order messages cannot leave a tab on an older version. Full state or every note is copied into every tab on each edit, and a session token does not belong in a message any script on the origin can receive.

questions.prompt: Order how a leader tab hands over when it closes.

items.label: A waiting tab acquires the lock
The leader tab closes
The new leader opens the connection and relays updates
Its lock is released

questions.explanation: Holding the lock defines the leader, so releasing it is the hand-over.

questions.prompt: Users keep about 4 tabs of an app open; 200,000 users are online. How many live connections does the server see without a leader tab?
assumptions: Each tab opens one connection without coordination
questions.explanation: Sanity check: with a leader tab it would be about 200,000, a quarter of the load.

flashcards.back: Each tab has its own memory; only storage is shared.
A broadcast channel, or storage events for local storage changes.
Elect a leader tab with a named lock; another takes over when it closes.

mechanism.title: How tabs of one origin share and coordinate
steps: Tabs, windows and workers of one origin each run as separate programs with their own memory. They share storage, such as cookies, local storage and IndexedDB, and the HTTP cache, but not memory. A change in storage does not by itself redraw another tab.

Browsers provide signals. A storage event fires in other same-origin tabs when local storage changes. The Broadcast Channel API lets any same-origin context post a message to a named channel and receive messages from others on it. Messages are structured copies, so they should be small.

A common pattern writes the change to shared storage first, then posts a message with the item’s id and version. Receivers read the item from storage and apply it only if the version is newer than what they show, which tolerates messages arriving late or twice.

Some work should run once per user, not once per tab: a live connection, a sync loop, a periodic poll. The Web Locks API grants a named lock to one context at a time. The holder acts as leader; others wait for the same lock. When the holder’s tab closes, its lock is released and the next waiter becomes leader.

Shared and service workers are alternatives: a shared worker can hold one connection for all tabs, and a service worker can intercept requests and message clients. They add their own lifetimes and browser support differences, so many apps combine a lock-elected leader with broadcast messages.

useWhen: Apps users keep open in several tabs: mail, chat, dashboards, documents.
Logout, theme and settings changes that must apply everywhere.
avoidWhen: Avoid one live connection per tab when one per user would do.
Avoid sending large state blobs between tabs.

rows: Local storage only; not fired in the writing tab
No delivery to closed tabs; no ordering across sources
Hand-over gap when the leader closes

numbers.title: Connections with and without a leader tab
assumptions: One live connection per tab without coordination
steps: Without a leader: 200,000 × 4 = 800,000 connections.
With a leader: one per user, about 200,000.
The server holds a quarter of the connections and sends each update once per user.
Other tabs get updates over the broadcast channel at no server cost.
numbers.result: Leader election turns per-tab cost into per-user cost.

india.title: What browsers provide
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: MDN documents the Broadcast Channel API as allowing basic communication between browsing contexts, such as windows and tabs, and workers on the same origin. It documents the Web Locks API as letting scripts in one tab or worker asynchronously acquire a lock, hold it while work is performed, then release it, so that only one context holds a given lock at a time.

pitfalls.trap: “IndexedDB is shared, so tabs stay in sync.”
pitfalls.say: “Storage is shared but screens aren’t; I’d broadcast a change message so other tabs reload.”
“I’d elect one leader tab with a lock to hold the socket and relay updates.”

takeaways: Tabs share storage, not memory.
Write to storage, then broadcast an id and version.
Elect a leader tab with a lock for work that should run once.
Apply only newer versions so late or repeated messages are harmless.

interactive.title: Logout in one of five tabs
interactive.prompt: A user has five tabs of a mail app open and clicks “Log out” in one. The app clears the session cookie but sends no message to other tabs. What do the other four tabs show?

choices.label: The sign-in screen straight away
choices.feedback: Nothing tells them to change; their screens are separate programs.

choices.label: The inbox, until they next make a request that fails
choices.feedback: Right: their in-memory data stays visible until a request is rejected or they are told.

choices.label: A blank page, as the browser wipes them
choices.feedback: Clearing a cookie does not clear other tabs’ memory or screens.

interactive.reveal: Post a “logged-out” message on a broadcast channel so every tab clears its data and shows sign-in at once. Private data should not stay on screen in tabs the user forgot about.

seeAlso.why: Service workers, another way to share work across tabs
Live connections a leader tab can own

title: Rendering Huge Lists: Virtualization
objectives: Explain why rendering every row of a long list is slow
Render only the visible window of rows plus a small overscan
Handle variable row heights, scroll position, search and accessibility

cards.title: Ten thousand rows, twenty on screen
cards.body: A list of 10,000 rows with 8 elements each creates 80,000 elements, yet only about 20 rows fit on screen. Every element costs memory, style and layout work, so the page loads slowly and scrolls badly. Virtualization renders only the rows near the viewport and reuses them as the user scrolls.

cards.title: Worked example: the window
cards.body: Rows are 48 px tall and the viewport is 800 px, so about 17 rows are visible (18 when scrolled mid-row). Adding 5 rows of overscan above and below gives 27 rendered rows, and 27 × 8 = 216 elements instead of 80,000. A tall spacer keeps the scrollbar the size of the full list, and the rows move to wherever the user has scrolled.

cards.title: How a virtual list renders
cards.body: Turn the scroll position into a range of rows.
steps: Read the scroll offset of the list container
First row = offset ÷ row height, minus the overscan
Last row = first row + rows that fit, plus the overscan
Render only those rows, positioned at their offsets
A spacer keeps the full height so the scrollbar is right

cards.title: Variable heights, and a lighter option
cards.body: If rows differ in height, estimate them, measure each row once it renders, and correct the offsets. For mostly static long pages, content-visibility (see How Browsers Render a Page) skips rendering work off screen while keeping the content findable and accessible, which virtualization does not.

cards.title: Trap: losing find-in-page and screen readers
cards.body: Rows that are not rendered cannot be found with the browser’s find-in-page or read by assistive technology. Provide your own search, keep the list’s total size and each row’s position available to assistive technology, and do not virtualize short lists that would render fine.

questions.prompt: A table renders 5,000 rows with 10 elements each. What is the main cost?

choices.label: Network time to download all of the row data first
About 50,000 elements to style, lay out and hold
The database query that produces the rows
Decoding the icon images shown in the rows

questions.explanation: About 50,000 elements must each be styled, laid out and kept in memory, and layout work grows with that count. The row data is typically a few hundred kilobytes, the query runs once on the server, and the icons are usually a handful of cached images.

questions.prompt: An order-history page lists 10,000 orders in a virtual list. A tester scrolls to order 5,000 and inspects the page. What should the DOM contain?

choices.label: About 27 rows near order 5,000 inside one tall spacer
All 10,000 rows, most hidden with display: none
Rows 1 to 5,027, the early ones scrolled out of view
Only the 17 rows that are fully visible, no others

questions.explanation: A virtual list keeps only the visible window plus overscan (about 17 + 10 rows at 48 px in an 800 px viewport) and a spacer for the full height. Hiding rows with styles keeps all 80,000 elements; keeping every row above the window grows without limit as you scroll; and with no overscan a fast flick shows blank space.

questions.prompt: Why add overscan rows outside the viewport?

choices.label: To keep the scrollbar thumb the right size for the list
To help search engines index the list
So fast scrolling shows rows instead of blank space
To reduce the number of elements rendered

questions.explanation: Overscan rows are already rendered when a fast flick brings them into view, so no blank gap shows. The spacer, not overscan, keeps the scrollbar the right size; search engines do not see virtual rows either way; and overscan adds a few elements rather than removing any.

questions.prompt: What is a real drawback of virtualizing a list?

choices.label: The scrollbar size can no longer match the length of the list
Rows can no longer contain links
Images in rows stop loading lazily
Find-in-page and assistive technology miss rows not rendered

questions.explanation: Unrendered rows are not in the document, so find-in-page and screen readers cannot reach them: provide your own search and expose the list size and each row’s position. The spacer keeps the scrollbar right, rendered rows can hold links, and lazy images still work in the rows that render.

questions.prompt: Order what happens on each scroll in a virtual list.

items.label: Render or reuse elements for those rows
Read the scroll offset
Position them at their offsets inside the spacer
Compute the first and last rows, with overscan

questions.explanation: Offset to range, range to elements, elements to positions.

questions.prompt: Rows are 48 px, the viewport is 800 px and overscan is 5 rows on each side. About how many rows does a virtual list render?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a few dozen rows whatever the list length.

flashcards.back: Elements cost style, layout and memory; render only what is near the viewport.
A spacer as tall as the full list.
Find-in-page and assistive technology miss unrendered rows.

sources.title: Chrome for Developers: Avoid an excessive DOM size

mechanism.title: How a virtual list keeps the element count fixed
steps: Every element on the page has a cost. The browser matches style rules against it, computes its layout box, and keeps it in memory; changes near the top of a long list can force layout of everything after. Lighthouse’s guidance flags pages with very large element counts because they slow loading, interaction and memory.

A virtual list keeps a scroll container whose inner spacer is as tall as all rows together, so the scrollbar behaves as if every row existed. On scroll, it reads the offset, works out which rows intersect the viewport, and renders only those, plus some overscan above and below.

Rendered rows are positioned at their offsets inside the spacer, usually with a transform or absolute positioning. Elements leaving the window are reused for rows entering it, so the number of elements stays roughly constant however long the list grows. Reuse also avoids creating and discarding thousands of elements during a long, fast scroll.

Variable row heights need a model of offsets. A list starts with estimated heights, measures rows after they render, and updates the offsets of rows below. Keeping the scroll position anchored to the row the user is reading avoids jumps when estimates are corrected.

Accessibility and search need explicit work. Rows outside the window are absent from the document, so find-in-page misses them and assistive technology cannot count them. Lists can expose their total size and each row’s position with ARIA attributes, keep focus on a rendered row, and offer an in-app search. Printing and copying a whole selection need the same care, since only rendered rows can be printed or selected.

useWhen: Lists, tables and feeds with thousands of rows or more.
Long chat histories and logs that grow while open.
avoidWhen: Avoid for short lists that render well as they are.
Avoid when users rely on find-in-page and you cannot provide search.

rows: Slow load and scroll on long lists

numbers.title: Elements with and without a window
steps: Render every row: 10,000 × 8 = 80,000 elements.
Visible rows: 800 ÷ 48 rounds up to 17.
Rendered rows: 17 + 10 = 27.
Virtualized: 27 × 8 = 216 elements.
numbers.result: The virtual list renders a few hundred elements whether the list holds a thousand rows or a million.

india.title: What the tools report
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Chrome’s Lighthouse documentation for the excessive DOM size audit says it warns when a page’s body has more than about 800 elements and errors above about 1,400, and explains that a large DOM increases memory use, style calculation and layout cost. web.dev documents the content-visibility property, which lets the browser skip rendering work for off-screen content.

pitfalls.trap: “The browser only paints what’s on screen, so 80,000 rows is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “Style, layout and memory still scale with every element; I’d render a window.”
“Only long ones; it costs find-in-page and needs accessibility work.”

takeaways: Element count drives style, layout and memory cost.
Render the visible window plus overscan inside a full-height spacer.
Measure variable rows and anchor the scroll position.
Restore search and accessibility that unrendered rows lose.

interactive.title: How many elements?
interactive.prompt: Rows are 48 px tall with 8 elements each, the viewport is 800 px and the list renders 5 extra rows above and below. Slide the list length and compare rendering every row with a virtual list.
interactive.takeaway: Rendering every row passes the 1,400 elements Lighthouse flags at fewer than 200 rows; the virtual list stays at 216 elements however long the list grows.

seeAlso.why: Memory that grows with long-lived lists
Transforms that keep scrolling rows on the compositor
Rendering cost per element and content-visibility

title: Layout Thrashing and Layout Shift
objectives: Explain forced synchronous layout and why interleaved reads and writes are slow
Prevent layout shift by reserving space, and read a CLS score

cards.title: Recap: a read after a write forces layout
cards.body: How Browsers Render a Page explained forced synchronous layout. The pattern to spot here is the loop: write a style, read a size, repeat. Each pass forces a fresh layout, so the cost grows with the number of items: layout thrashing.

cards.title: Worked example: 200 cards
cards.body: A script sets the width of 200 cards, reading each card’s height right after setting it. If one forced layout takes about 0.25 ms on this page (illustrative), 200 × 0.25 ms = 50 ms, three frames at 60 per second. Reading all 200 heights first, then setting all widths, needs one layout.

cards.title: Reads, then writes
cards.body: Group by kind so the browser lays out once.
steps: Read every measurement you need
Compute new values in memory
Write every style change
Let the browser lay out once before the next frame
Defer any further reads to the next frame

cards.title: Layout shift is the user-visible cousin
cards.body: Cumulative Layout Shift measures content moving unexpectedly, such as text pushed down by an image or banner that loads late. A shift that affects half the viewport and moves content by a quarter of its height scores 0.5 × 0.25 = 0.125, above the 0.1 that counts as good. Reserving space for media, ads and embeds prevents most shifts.

cards.title: Trap: animating layout properties
cards.body: Animating width, height or top changes layout on every frame. Animating transform and opacity usually skips layout and paint, and shifts caused by transforms do not count towards CLS. Move things with transforms, not with layout properties.

questions.prompt: Right after a script changes a card’s width, which read does not force the browser to lay out the page?

choices.label: Reading the card’s rendered height
Reading the card’s position on the page
Reading how far its container is scrolled
Reading a width the script saved earlier

questions.explanation: Any geometry read (size, position, scroll offset) needs current layout, so after a write it forces one. A value already held in the script’s memory needs nothing from the browser, which is why measuring once before the loop and reusing the numbers removes the thrashing.

questions.prompt: How should a loop that resizes 200 cards based on their heights be structured?

choices.label: Write then read for each card in turn
Spread the cards over 200 separate frames
Read all heights first, then write all sizes
Hide the cards while resizing them one by one

questions.explanation: Batched, the loop costs one layout instead of 200, about 50 ms saved at 0.25 ms each (three dropped frames). Spreading the cards over 200 frames takes more than 3 seconds to finish, and hiding cards while resizing them one by one still interleaves reads and writes.

questions.prompt: A late ad pushes the article down. What prevents the shift?

choices.label: Loading the ad sooner with a higher priority
Reserving the ad’s space before it loads
Fading the ad in slowly
Showing the ad only after the user scrolls

questions.explanation: Reserved space, such as fixed dimensions or an aspect ratio on the ad slot, means nothing moves when the ad arrives. Loading it sooner only narrows the window for the shift, fading changes opacity while the layout still jumps, and showing ads after a scroll shifts content that is now on screen.

questions.prompt: Which change is least likely to add to CLS?

choices.label: An image with no width and height loading late
A web font swapping in with very different metrics
A banner inserted above content after load
A menu sliding in with a transform

questions.explanation: Moving an element with transform does not change layout, so it is not counted as a layout shift. A late image without dimensions, a font with different metrics and a banner inserted above content all move content that was already laid out.

questions.prompt: Order one frame of a batched DOM update.

items.label: Compute new values in memory
Let the browser lay out and paint once
Write every style change
Read every measurement needed

questions.explanation: All reads, then computation, then all writes, then one layout.

questions.prompt: A shift affects half the viewport and moves content by a quarter of the viewport height. What is its layout shift score?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: one shift like this already exceeds the 0.1 “good” threshold.

flashcards.back: Interleaved writes and reads forcing a layout each time.
Batch all reads, then all writes.
0.1 or less; reserve space and move things with transforms.

sources.title: web.dev: Avoid large, complex layouts and layout thrashing

mechanism.title: Why the order of reads and writes matters
steps: A frame runs script, then recalculates style, lays out boxes, paints and composites. The browser marks layout as dirty when styles change and normally recomputes it once, just before painting the next frame.

Reading geometry, such as an element’s height, offset or scroll position, needs current layout. If layout is dirty, the browser must run style and layout immediately inside the script: a forced synchronous layout. In a loop that alternates writes and reads, each iteration dirties layout and then forces it again.

Batching restores one layout per frame: perform all reads first, compute, then perform all writes. Reads can be cached between frames, and writes scheduled for just before the next frame. Smaller layout scopes, such as containment on independent components, also shrink the cost of each layout.

Layout shift is a separate, user-visible problem. When content moves without user input, each shift is scored as impact fraction, the share of the viewport affected, times distance fraction, how far things moved relative to the viewport. Cumulative Layout Shift reports the largest burst of such shifts during the page’s life.

Most shifts come from content arriving without reserved space: images and video without dimensions, ads and embeds, late banners, and web fonts with different metrics. Setting width and height or an aspect ratio, reserving slots, and inserting new content below the viewport or in response to user input avoid them. Shifts within half a second of a tap or key press are excluded from the score.

useWhen: Scripts that measure and then change many elements, such as masonry grids and auto-sizing text.
Pages with images, ads, embeds or late-loading banners.
avoidWhen: Avoid alternating style writes and geometry reads in loops.
Avoid animating width, height, top or left when a transform would do.

rows: No layout and no layout shift

numbers.title: Cost of thrashing and of one shift
assumptions: Shift affects 0.5 of the viewport and moves 0.25 of its height
steps: Interleaved: 200 × 0.25 ms = 50 ms of layout, about three 60 Hz frames.
Batched: one layout, about 0.25 ms.
Good CLS is 0.1 or less, so this single shift fails it.
numbers.result: Batching turns a per-item cost into a per-frame cost; reserving space removes the shift entirely.

india.title: Thresholds from the guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: web.dev defines Cumulative Layout Shift as a Core Web Vital, with 0.1 or less considered good and more than 0.25 poor, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads. Its guidance on layout thrashing explains that reading layout properties after changing styles forces synchronous layout, and recommends batching reads before writes.

pitfalls.trap: “The loop is only 200 items, it can’t be slow.”
pitfalls.say: “Interleaving forces 200 layouts; I’d read everything first, then write.”

pitfalls.trap: “The image loads fast, so no space is needed.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d set its dimensions; any late load otherwise shifts the page.”

takeaways: A read after a write forces layout immediately.
Batch reads, then writes, for one layout per frame.
CLS is impact times distance; 0.1 or less is good.
Reserve space for late content and move things with transforms.

interactive.title: Interleaved or batched?
interactive.prompt: A loop updates some cards, reading each one’s height right after changing its width. Each forced layout costs about 0.25 ms here (illustrative) and a frame at 60 Hz has 16.7 ms. Slide the number of cards.
interactive.takeaway: Past about 66 cards the interleaved loop overruns a frame on layout alone; batching reads before writes keeps it to one layout.

seeAlso.why: How normal flow, flexbox and grid lay out boxes

title: Long Tasks, Web Workers and INP
objectives: Explain how a long task on the main thread delays input
Split work into short tasks or move it to a worker
Read INP thresholds and find what drives a poor score

cards.title: One thread handles taps and your code
cards.body: The main thread runs scripts, handles input, and renders. While a task runs, a tap waits in the queue. A task longer than 50 ms counts as a long task, and a 400 ms task means a tap at its start waits 400 ms before any handler runs, and longer before the screen changes.

cards.title: Worked example: filtering 50,000 rows
cards.body: Filtering and sorting 50,000 rows takes 400 ms on a mid-range phone (illustrative). Split into 50 ms pieces, 400 ÷ 50 gives 8 pieces, with input handled between them, so a tap waits at most about 50 ms. Moved to a worker, the main thread stays free and the tap is handled at once while the filter finishes elsewhere.

cards.title: Keeping input responsive
cards.body: Shorten main-thread tasks or move them off it.
steps: Find long tasks in a performance trace
Do the visible update first, defer the rest
Split remaining work into short chunks that yield
Move heavy computation to a worker and post results back
Measure INP from real users afterwards

cards.title: What workers can and cannot do
cards.body: A web worker runs script on another thread with its own memory. It can compute, parse and fetch, but it cannot touch the page’s elements; it posts messages, which are copied, back to the main thread. Large data can be transferred rather than copied. Workers suit pure computation, not rendering.

cards.title: Trap: fast on your laptop
cards.body: A 60 ms task on a fast laptop can take several times longer on a budget phone. INP is judged at the 75th percentile of real visits, so test on slower devices or with CPU throttling, and watch field data rather than one local run.

questions.prompt: A 300 ms task starts just before a user taps a button. What happens to the tap?

choices.label: It interrupts the running task and its handler runs first
It waits until the task finishes before its handler runs
It is dropped and must be repeated
It runs in parallel on another thread

questions.explanation: Input is queued behind the running task on the main thread.

questions.prompt: Which job suits a web worker best?

choices.label: Parsing and sorting a large data file
Changing the colour of a button on hover
Measuring the height of a list item
Moving focus to a dialog

questions.explanation: Workers do computation; changes to page elements must happen on the main thread.

questions.prompt: Users say a dashboard feels sluggish after each click. Which delay does the responsiveness vital capture?

choices.label: Time until the largest image or text block appears
How far visible content moves while the page is loading
Script download time for the page
Delay from an interaction to the next painted frame

questions.explanation: INP covers input delay, handler time and rendering for interactions across the visit.

questions.prompt: Why split a 400 ms task into 50 ms pieces that yield between them?

choices.label: The total work finishes sooner because pieces are smaller
The browser then runs pieces on several cores
Input can be handled between pieces, so taps wait less
Long tasks are blocked by the browser

questions.explanation: Yielding lets queued input run; total time stays about the same.

questions.prompt: Order the response to a slow interaction.

items.label: Split or move the remaining work
Find the long task in a trace
Confirm with field INP data
Paint the visible feedback first

questions.explanation: Measure, give feedback quickly, fix the heavy part, then confirm with real users.

questions.prompt: Good INP is 200 ms. A tap’s handler and the next paint take 80 ms together. If a tap can arrive just as a main-thread chunk starts, what is the longest chunk that still meets 200 ms?
assumptions: The tap waits for one whole chunk
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 120 ms is the ceiling, not a target; 50 ms chunks leave margin for slower phones.

flashcards.back: A main-thread task over 50 ms; input waits behind it.
200 ms or less at the 75th percentile; over 500 ms is poor.
Own thread and memory, no access to page elements; talks by messages.

mechanism.title: How input waits and how to shorten the wait
steps: The main thread runs one task at a time from its queues: script, input events, timers and rendering steps. A task is not interrupted when input arrives; the input event becomes a task that runs after the current one ends. Tasks over 50 ms are reported as long tasks.

An interaction has three parts: input delay, waiting for the main thread to be free; processing time, running the handlers; and presentation delay, until the browser paints the next frame. Interaction to Next Paint reports roughly the slowest interaction of a visit, so one heavy handler can define the score.

Yielding splits work so other tasks can run between pieces. The code does a chunk, schedules the rest as a new task, and returns; queued input runs in the gap. Total work is unchanged or slightly higher, but the longest wait shrinks to about one chunk.

Workers move computation off the main thread. A dedicated worker has its own event loop and memory and communicates by posting messages, which are copied with the structured clone algorithm unless buffers are transferred. Workers cannot access page elements, so the main thread still applies results to the page.

In handlers, update what the user sees first, such as a pressed state or spinner, and defer non-urgent work like analytics or saving. Reducing rendering cost, such as large layouts after an update, shortens the presentation part. Field data at the 75th percentile shows whether real users benefit.

useWhen: Pages with heavy parsing, filtering, sorting or formatting on interaction.
Apps targeting mid-range and low-end phones.
avoidWhen: Avoid workers for small tasks where message copying costs more than the work.
Avoid one long handler that updates the screen and does all background work in the same task.

rows: Slightly more total time, chunking logic

numbers.title: How long a tap can wait
assumptions: Filtering task of 400 ms on a mid-range phone (illustrative)
Good INP is 200 ms or less
steps: One task: a tap at its start waits about 400 ms, past the 200 ms good threshold before any handler runs.
Split: 400 ÷ 50 gives 8 pieces; the worst wait is about 50 ms.
Worker: the main thread is free; the wait is set by other work only.
Total filter time stays about 400 ms in every case.
numbers.result: Splitting or moving work does not make it faster; it stops it from blocking input.

india.title: Thresholds from the guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: web.dev defines Interaction to Next Paint as a Core Web Vital, with 200 ms or less considered good and more than 500 ms poor, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads. Its guidance on long tasks describes tasks longer than 50 ms as long tasks and recommends breaking them up and yielding to the main thread. MDN documents web workers as running scripts in background threads that communicate by messages.

pitfalls.trap: “The filter is slow, so we need a faster algorithm.”
pitfalls.say: “Maybe, but first I’d stop it blocking input by yielding or moving it to a worker.”
“They can’t touch page elements; the worker computes and posts results back.”

takeaways: Input waits behind whatever task is running.
Long tasks are over 50 ms; good INP is 200 ms or less.
Split work and yield, or move computation to a worker.
Update visible feedback first and measure with field data.

interactive.title: How long does a tap wait?
interactive.prompt: A filter runs as one task on the main thread. Good INP is 200 ms or less, and the fix splits work into 50 ms pieces or moves it to a worker. Slide the task length.
interactive.takeaway: A single task over 200 ms fails the good INP threshold through input delay alone; split or moved, the worst wait stays near 50 ms whatever the task length.

seeAlso.why: Long-lived pages where workers hold memory
Loading less script so the main thread is free sooner
The event loop and task queues behind long tasks
